sections.section_title: The Fifth Trumpet -- The Star and the Abyss
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that a fallen star receives the key to the bottomless pit by divine authorization (the divine passive edothe) and opens it, releasing smoke that darkens the sun and air, with imagery drawn from Genesis 19:28 (Sodom's destruction) and Exodus 19:18 (Sinai theophany).

The neutral reading found that locusts from the abyss are commanded not to harm vegetation but only those who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads, establishing that the sealing from chapter 7 provides operative, functional protection from judgment for God's servants.
sections.relevance: God's seal provides effective, concrete protection for his people within the scene of devastating judgment. The sealed are not removed from the world but are preserved through the judgment, replicating the exodus pattern where the blood on the doorposts protected Israel's firstborn from the destroyer (Exodus 12:13) and the mark on the foreheads protected the righteous in Ezekiel 9:4-6. This demonstrates God's active commitment to preserving those who bear his mark of ownership.
key_phrases: only the men who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads
They were told not to hurt the grass of the earth, nor any green thing, nor any tree

sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the locusts are described as a composite creature combining features of horses, humans, women, lions, scorpions, and insects, drawing extensively on Joel 2:4-5 and constructing a symbolic vision of overwhelming spiritual torment that defies literal interpretation and demands symbolic reading.

The neutral reading found that the locust king is named Abaddon in Hebrew (Destruction) and Apollyon in Greek (Destroyer), personifying the destroying power of the abyss, with a phonetic echo of Apollo that would have been audible to Greek-speaking audiences in Asia Minor.

The neutral reading found that this transitional verse marks the completion of the first woe (fifth trumpet) and announces two remaining woes, functioning as a structural marker orienting the audience and signaling further escalation.

sections.section_title: The Sixth Trumpet -- The Four Angels at the Euphrates
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that a voice from the golden altar (the same altar where the saints' prayers were offered in 8:3-5) commands the release of four angels bound at the Euphrates, prepared for an exact hour, day, month, and year to kill a third of mankind, with every element operating under precise divine foreordination.

sections.section_title: The Cavalry of Fire, Smoke, and Brimstone
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that a cavalry of 200 million horse-like creatures breathes fire, smoke, and brimstone, killing a third of mankind, with the imagery combining military terror and Sodom-destruction vocabulary (Genesis 19:24) into a vision of judgment that exceeds any conceivable human army.

The neutral reading found that the survivors of the trumpet plagues refuse to repent of idolatry (worshiping demons and idols that can neither see nor hear nor walk) and moral wickedness (murders, sorceries, immorality, thefts), paralleling Pharaoh's hardening during the Egyptian plagues and standing as the theological climax of the chapter.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading identifies this as the dark counterpart to the repentance demanded of the assemblies in chapters 2-3 and explicitly states that 'the document does not assume that its audience will automatically be among the saved; it places the choice before them with unflinching clarity.' The same word metanoeo (repent) that the risen Christ used to call the assemblies to repentance (2:5, 16, 21-22; 3:3, 19) is the response the earth-dwellers refuse to give. The contrast between the two groups implies that the assemblies' standing depends on their response to the call for repentance -- repentance is presented as the necessary and expected response to divine warning, and its refusal leads to continued judgment.
key_phrases: did not repent of the works of their hands
they did not repent of their murders nor of their sorceries nor of their immorality nor of their thefts
which can neither see nor hear nor walk
